basis: thanksgiving for the holy name dwelling in hearts
note: The eucharistic prayer thanks the Father for his holy name dwelling in believers' hearts; this joins prayer, gratitude, God's name, and inward remembrance.

basis: hallowing God's name in the Lord's Prayer
note: The Didache prescribes the Lord's Prayer, which asks that the Father's name be hallowed; this is a concrete Christian liturgical form of praise within prayer.

basis: Lord's Prayer formula; hallowing the Name
note: The Didache transmits the Lord's Prayer as the form believers are to pray, including the hallowing of the Father's name. It supplies the early Christian liturgical text that its following thrice-daily rule presupposes.
The Didache tells its readers to pray this prayer three times a day; this shows remembrance and praise of the name as repeated verbal practice.

basis: reciting the Lord's Prayer three times daily
note: The Didache turns the Lord's Prayer into a thrice-daily discipline. This early Christian rule offers a concrete liturgical counterpart to the commentary's repeated prayer and remembrance around the day.

Justin describes Scripture being read, the leader exhorting hearers, and all standing together to pray; this concrete service sequence matches the commentary's reading, reminder, and prayer as one practice.

basis: praying and singing with spirit and mind
note: Paul says he will pray and sing both with spirit and with mind; this concretely unites verbal prayer, praise, and inward intention.

basis: praying and singing praise with spirit and mind
note: Paul deliberately pairs prayer and praise in both spirit and mind, providing a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's unified tesbih, remembrance, and prayer with intentional participation.

basis: an audible blessing needs an intelligible Amen
note: Paul asks how an outsider can say Amen to a blessing if he does not know what was said; this makes the public, voiced character of liturgical prayer explicit.

basis: secrets of the heart; falling face-down; worship and confession
note: When hidden heart-secrets are disclosed, the hearer falls on his face, worships God, and declares God truly present. This unusually combines the commentary's hidden/open axis, prostration, and voiced God-remembrance.
God forgives and cleanses those who confess; it provides a specific Christian pairing of spoken penitential address and divine purification relevant to the commentary's 14–15 relation.
Paul's short command to pray continually makes devotion an ongoing practice, alongside the commentary's recurring remembrance.
The command to pray without ceasing provides a Christian analogue to the commentary's repeated, abundant tesbih and remembrance, although it does not prescribe the same ritual form.
The next command is to give thanks in everything; this makes thanksgiving an explicit companion to continual prayer.

The verse deliberately lists supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings. It supplies a close Christian comparison to the commentary's semantic expansion of salat and dhikr into du'a, praise, and thanks.
Paul directs men to pray everywhere, lifting holy hands; this is a specific posture for the bodily prayer described in the commentary.

basis: prayer everywhere; lifted holy hands; moral restraint
note: The instruction to pray everywhere with lifted holy hands is joined to rejection of anger and disputing. It connects the commentary's bodily prayer with its ethical claim that prayer opposes wrongdoing.

basis: prayers and alms as a memorial before God
note: Cornelius's prayers and alms ascend as a memorial before God. The passage gives a striking New Testament link between remembrance, prayer, and obedient action, matching the commentary's broad account of dhikr.
At midnight Paul and Silas are praying and singing hymns to God; this concretely treats supplication and praise as one devotional act.

basis: praying and hymn-singing heard by others
note: Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight, with prisoners listening; this is a specific scene of the vocal, audible devotional practice developed from jahr in the commentary.
The verse promises salvation to everyone who calls on the Lord's name; this treats invocation of the name as an act of devotion, as in 87:15.

basis: teaching and prayers in the community
note: The first believers devote themselves to apostolic teaching and to prayers; this places recitation/admonition and prayer in the same communal practice.

basis: washing away sins while calling on the Name
note: Paul is told to be washed from sins while calling on the Lord's name. It specifically joins name-invocation to cleansing, a close Christian meeting of the commentary's remembrance and divine purification relation.
Peter and John go up together to the temple at the appointed hour of prayer. The scene offers a specific communal, timed counterpart to the commentary's recurring prayer and praise.
Stephen calls on the Lord Jesus as he entrusts his spirit to him; this is a specific invocation of the Lord's name within prayer.

basis: kneeling and crying loudly in prayer
note: Stephen kneels and cries with a loud voice for his killers' forgiveness; this joins bodily posture, audible prayer, and supplication.

Christ's word is to dwell richly as believers teach and admonish one another through psalms and hymns, singing with gratitude; this closely matches the commentary's sequence of recitation, reminder, and prayer.

basis: word dwelling, teaching and admonition, psalms and gratitude
note: The verse puts instruction and admonition together with psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and gratitude; it closely resembles the commentary's intervening recitation, reminder, and worship as one practice.

basis: word and deed in the Name; thanksgiving
note: Whatever is done in word or deed is to be done in the Lord's name with thanks. This directly mirrors the commentary's integration of utterance, deed, Name, and gratitude under worship.
The community is told to persist in prayer, watchful with thanksgiving; this is a specific pairing of supplication and praise.
The community is told to speak to one another in psalms and hymns and sing to the Lord; this shows verbal recitation and song as shared worship.

basis: psalms and hymns spoken and sung in the heart
note: The exhortation joins speaking psalms and hymns with singing in the heart to the Lord; it reflects the commentary's double focus on vocal remembrance and inward devotion.
The next verse calls for continual thanks to God the Father in Jesus' name; this connects praise and remembrance with prayerful gratitude.

basis: drawing near; hearts sprinkled clean; bodies washed
note: Hebrews couples approach to God with a true heart and imagery of cleansed hearts and washed bodies. It provides a Christian purification-and-worship analogue to the commentary's 87:14–15 association.

basis: praise from lips confessing the name
note: The passage calls praise a sacrifice offered to God, the fruit of lips confessing his name; this directly joins verbal praise, the divine name, and worship.

basis: sacrifice of praise; fruit of lips confessing the Name
note: Hebrews calls continual praise the fruit of lips that confess God's name; it closely matches the commentary's dhikr as the Name on the tongue and tesbih as worship.

basis: doing good and sharing as sacrifices pleasing to God
note: This verse calls concrete beneficence and sharing sacrifices pleasing to God. It extends the commentary's word-action-intention account of worship to an explicitly ethical Christian practice.

basis: prayer in suffering, praise in joy
note: James directs the suffering person to pray and the cheerful person to sing praise; this shows prayer and praise as closely related responses within lived practice.
Before raising Lazarus, Jesus looks upward and thanks the Father; this is audible prayer in a public scene.
Jesus explains that he spoke for the surrounding crowd to believe; this qualifies the warning against performative prayer by showing an aloud prayer directed to others' understanding.

Jesus identifies true worship with spirit and truth. It gives an interpretive complement to the commentary's refusal to reduce worship to bodily movement or spoken formula, while retaining worship as an enacted practice.

basis: the people praying at the hour of incense
note: The whole assembled multitude prays outside during the incense hour. It offers a precise communal and timed liturgical counterpart to the commentary's formal prayer practice.
When Zechariah's mouth opens and his tongue is freed, he speaks blessing to God; this gives a concrete scene of the tongue becoming an instrument of praise.
The Pharisee thanks God while boasting of his own righteousness; this gives a specific case where prayer's words do not express the inward devotion emphasized by the commentary.
The tax collector stands at a distance, will not lift his eyes, beats his breast, and asks God for mercy; this joins bodily posture and prayer with inward humility.

basis: bodily humility and a plea for mercy
note: The tax collector stands at a distance, lowers his eyes, beats his breast, and asks God for mercy; it supplies a concrete Christian scene in which bodily prayer and du'a-like petition are inseparable.

Jesus says the tax collector, rather than the Pharisee, goes home justified; this makes the quality of the person praying matter, like the commentary's distinction between successful devotion and negligent prayer.

basis: night-and-day service with fasting and prayers
note: Anna serves God night and day through fasting and prayers. Her recurring discipline meets the commentary's abundant remembrance and continuing worship without reducing it to one isolated prayer.
Jesus kneels on the Mount of Olives and prays; this is a direct bodily instance of the prayer movement described in the commentary.
Jesus repeatedly withdraws to deserted places to pray; this is a specific secluded form of the prayer whose hidden dimension God knows in 87:7.
Jesus rises while it is still dark and prays in a solitary place. This is a specific Christian scene for the commentary's praise and prayer before the sun's rising.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's lips-honor/heart-distant charge against people who worship in vain; this Christian reading makes inward intention a test of outward religious practice.

Jesus applies Isaiah's lips-and-heart critique to a dispute about worship and tradition. It provides a Christian interpretive development of the commentary's contrast between tongue-level mention and wholehearted, attentive worship.

The continuation of Jesus' Isaiah citation calls worship vain when it teaches merely human precepts. It gives the explicit Christian continuation needed for the commentary's concern with heedless or merely external worship.

basis: falling on the face and praying
note: Jesus falls on his face and prays in Gethsemane, an explicit conjunction of prostrating posture and supplication comparable to the prayer movements named in the commentary.
Jesus warns against praying at street corners to be seen by people; this supplies a concrete public-prayer case for 87:7's distinction between the voiced and hidden.

basis: public prayer performed to be seen
note: Jesus criticizes prayer offered for public display. In conjunction with the commentary's treatment of jahr as audible prayer, it makes intention rather than volume the relevant ethical distinction.

basis: prayer in secret seen by God
note: Jesus directs the disciple to pray in a closed room, where the Father sees in secret; this complements 87:7's claim that God knows what is concealed.

basis: prayer in secret; the Father seeing the hidden
note: Jesus directs prayer to the hidden place and grounds it in the Father's seeing what is hidden; this complements 87:7 as read in the commentary, where God knows both vocalized and concealed devotion.
Jesus' prayer begins “hallowed be your name”; this places sanctification of God's name inside the prayer practice that follows.

basis: hallowing the Father's name in prayer
note: Jesus' model prayer makes the hallowing of God's name its first petition, directly pairing prayer with the treatment of the divine name central to 87:1 and 87:15.
The hymn says every knee bends at Jesus' name; this joins bodily prostration to the honor of the Lord's name.

basis: bowing every knee at a name
note: In its Christological setting, the verse makes the response to Jesus' name a universal bending of knees; it is a precise Christian meeting of named confession and the bodily prayer emphasized in the commentary.
The hymn says every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord; this makes spoken confession of the Lord's name a universal act of praise.

basis: every tongue confessing to God's glory
note: The verse completes the preceding knee-bending with every tongue's confession to the glory of God the Father. It gives the verbal side of the name-and-body meeting already present in the commentary.
Paul joins prayer and supplication with thanksgiving in one act of address to God, closely echoing the commentary's salat as du'a and dhikr as praise and thanks.

basis: glorifying the Name and worship by all nations
note: The hymn asks who would not glorify the Lord's name and says all nations will come and worship. It directly pairs name-glorification with worship in a Christian doxological formula.
The elders hold incense bowls that are the prayers of the saints; this gives a Christian vision the same concrete prayer-as-incense image as the psalmic prayer tradition.

basis: falling in worship; harps; bowls identified as prayers
note: The elders fall before the Lamb while holding harps and bowls of incense identified as the saints' prayers. This heavenly liturgy joins body, praise music, and prayer in a form especially relevant to the commentary's single devotional practice.

basis: calling on the Lord's name and salvation
note: Paul's citation makes calling on the Lord's name the path to salvation; it gives a specific New Testament meeting with the commentary's sequence of remembering the Name, praying, and flourishing.

Paul describes offering bodies as a living sacrifice and worship; it gives a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's claim that worship includes bodily action as well as verbal and intentional devotion.
The Spirit intercedes with groanings too deep for words; this gives a specific hidden, nonverbal dimension to the commentary's contrast between what is voiced and concealed.
The one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's intention; this makes divine knowledge of what is inward explicit, as in 87:7.

basis: blessing the Name at light and darkness
note: The Rule of the Community schedules blessing God's name at the turning points of light and darkness, a close sectarian-Jewish analogue to the commentary's praise before sunrise and sunset.

basis: patriarchal derivation of fixed prayer times
note: The Talmud derives the three daily prayer services from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Its interpretive fixing of prayer in the day supplies a Jewish liturgical bridge to the commentary's praise at the sun's turning points.

basis: Hannah as model of silent prayer
note: The Talmud reads Hannah's moving lips and unheard voice as a model for prayer that is articulated yet inaudible; this sharpens the commentary's distinction between vocalized and concealed prayer.

basis: Hannah's moving lips and unraised voice
note: The Talmud reads Hannah's silent, lip-moving prayer as a source for how the Amidah is voiced. That interpretation makes the commentary's audible prayer or recitation and its hidden dimension a concrete liturgical question.

basis: Kaddish's sanctification of the great name
note: The Talmud's synagogue response asks that God's great name be blessed; this rabbinic liturgical formula makes praise of the name a communal prayer.

basis: a blessing requires God's Name and kingship
note: The rule that a blessing without the Name and kingship is no blessing makes formal invocation of the divine Name a defining liturgical act, a useful rabbinic counterpart to 87:1 and 87:15.

basis: magnifying and sanctifying the great Name
note: Kaddish begins by asking that God's great name be magnified and sanctified; its congregational formula directly stands beside 87:1's command to glorify the Lord's name.

basis: Torah reading, Shema, directing the heart
note: The Mishnah asks whether someone already reading Torah fulfils the Shema when its time comes, and makes the answer turn on directing the heart. It clarifies the commentary's claim that recitation can be remembrance and worship only with intention.
The Mishnah sets times for morning, afternoon, and evening prayer; this gives a concrete Jewish schedule for repeated prayer as a regular practice.

Rabbi Eliezer's dictum that a prayer made fixed is not supplication gives a Jewish interpretive counterpart to the commentary's explicit gloss that salat is du'a, while resisting prayer as empty routine.
The Mishnah says the pious waited before praying so they could direct their hearts to God; this joins inward intention to the bodily act, both included in the commentary's account of worship.

The early pietists pause before prayer in order to direct their hearts to their Father in heaven; this gives a concrete rabbinic practice for the commentary's inclusion of intention within tesbih and salat.

basis: public Torah and Shema recitation in temple liturgy
note: The daily temple order combines blessings with recitation of Torah passages and the Shema. It gives a concrete Jewish liturgical setting for the commentary's claim that scriptural reading is part of remembrance and worship.

On hearing the explicit Name from the high priest, priests and people kneel, prostrate, fall on their faces, and bless the Name; this rabbinic liturgy tightly combines the Name and the bodily acts named in the commentary.

basis: whole heart and voice; blessing the Lord's Name
note: Ben Sira tells hearers to give thanks with all heart and voice and bless the Lord's name. It is an unusually close Jewish synthesis of inward intent, vocal praise, and the Name.

basis: falling face-down before God Most High
note: The assembled people fall on their faces to worship the Almighty, God Most High; it brings together the commentary's epithet, public liturgy, and prostrating body.

basis: service of the heart interpreted as prayer
note: The Talmud asks what service is performed with the heart and answers, prayer. This interpretation directly illuminates the commentary's claim that worship includes intention as well as its audible and bodily forms.

basis: thanksgiving made known to the living
note: Raphael tells Tobit and Tobias to bless God and make God's goodness known among the living; this is a specific verbal enactment of praise and remembrance.
The worshiper ascribes glory due YHWH's name, brings an offering, and bows in holy array; this is a specific conjunction of praise and bodily ritual.

basis: glory due the Name; offering and worship
note: The verse moves from giving YHWH the glory due his name to bringing an offering and worshipping, closely matching the commentary's treatment of praise of the Name and formal worship as one practice.

basis: Elijah's spoken prayer at the offering
note: At the evening offering Elijah addresses YHWH by name and asks that Israel know he is God; this is a public, voiced prayer embedded in ritual worship.
Elijah asks YHWH to hear so the people will know him and their hearts will turn back; this joins invocation, response, and inward return in a single prayer.

basis: falling on faces; spoken confession of God
note: The people fall on their faces and voice a confession of YHWH; the verse joins the physical prostration and verbal God-remembrance that the commentary treats as a single act.

basis: standing before the altar; spreading hands toward heaven
note: Solomon stands before the altar in the assembled people's presence and spreads his hands heavenward. It supplies a specific biblical prayer posture alongside the commentary's standing and supplicatory movements.

Solomon asks God to hear prayer and supplication and to forgive. The verse gives a direct biblical meeting between human du'a-like appeal and the divine cleansing or forgiveness side of the commentary's 14–15 linkage.
Solomon asks God to hear from heaven and act because God alone knows each human heart; this gives a specific parallel to knowing what is hidden in 87:7.
Solomon finishes his prayer and supplication while kneeling with hands stretched toward heaven; this makes the commentary's bodily definition of prayer concrete.
Hannah prays in her heart while her lips move and her voice is not heard; this concretely distinguishes audible prayer from hidden devotion, matching 87:7's public and concealed.

basis: lips moving; voice unheard; inward prayer
note: Hannah speaks in her heart while her lips move and her voice is not heard; the contrast supplies a precise counterpart to the commentary's open vocal prayer or recitation and God's knowledge of what is hidden.
After the fire and glory appear, Israel bows face to the ground and worships; this gives a specific bodily response after prayer and offering.

basis: forced prostration to an image; fiery punishment
note: The verse orders bodily falling and worship under threat of a burning furnace. Alongside the commentary's prostration as Lord-directed prayer and its fire imagery, it makes the object and moral character of bodily worship decisive.
Daniel kneels three times daily, prays, and gives thanks to God; this is a specific repeated bodily practice joining prayer and praise.

Daniel's Aramaic form from צלי means “pray” beside the act of kneeling and giving thanks; it is a close Semitic counterpart to the commentary's ص ل و label, though the etymological relation to Arabic ṣalāt is uncertain.

basis: kneeling, prayer, thanksgiving, three daily times
note: Daniel kneels three times a day, prays, and gives thanks before his God, furnishing a specific counterpart to prayer as bodily movement, supplication, praise, and a recurring practice.

basis: Arabic ص ل و (B002/B003); Biblical Aramaic מְצַלֵּא
note: The commentary labels ص ل و as B002/B003. Daniel's Aramaic מְצַלֵּא, “praying,” is a close Aramaic-Syriac cognate form; its repeated kneeling and thanksgiving make the linguistic meeting concrete.

basis: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
note: The covenant song is to remain unforgotten from Israel's mouths; it supplies a concrete scriptural analogue to the commentary's movement from being made to recite to not forgetting and then reminding.
87:1 commands glorification of the Lord's name; Moses says that he will proclaim YHWH's name and calls his hearers to ascribe greatness to God, joining the two acts in one formula.
Israel is told to speak God's words at home, on the road, at lying down and rising; this is a specific scriptural practice of remembrance circulating on the tongue.

basis: Arabic ذ ك ر (B004/B005); Hebrew זכר
note: The commentary labels ذ ك ر as B004/B005 and develops remembering the Lord. Deuteronomy's זכר, “remember,” directs Israel to remember YHWH as the giver of power, a cognate used for faithful recollection rather than merely saying a word.
The speaker is warned not to rush words or heart in prayer before God; this adds a concrete caution about outward speech and inward attention to the commentary's account of vocal and hidden worship.
YHWH says he will come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; the Hebrew אזכיר uses זכר, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label, in a worship setting.
God promises presence and blessing at the altar where his name is remembered; this ties remembrance of the name to embodied worship.
YHWH says his name is for ever and his memorial through all generations; this makes the divine name itself an enduring object of remembrance beside 87:1 and 87:15.
The Hebrew זִכְרִי (“my memorial”) is from זכר, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label; here God's name is the memorial kept across generations.

basis: God sprinkling clean water and cleansing
note: Ezekiel depicts God cleansing the people from impurity. It does not itself define prayer, but it supplies the divine purification pole required by the commentary's linking of 87:14 to God's purifying salat.

basis: Aramaic צלי, prayer for the king
note: The Aramaic form מְצַלַּיִן means “they pray” for the king and his sons; it is a close Semitic counterpart to the commentary's ص ل و label, though the etymological relation to Arabic ṣalāt is uncertain.
The decree asks that temple offerings be made to heaven's God and prayers offered for the king; this places bodily cult and supplication together.
At the evening offering Ezra rises from his self-affliction, falls to his knees, and spreads his hands to God. Its timed and bodily prayer scene closely meets the commentary's descriptions of salat.
Melchizedek blesses God Most High after deliverance; the explicit divine title and blessing give a close Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's Lord Most High whose name is glorified.
God refuses many prayers while the worshippers' hands are full of blood; this gives a pointed ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that prayer turns people away from indecency and wrong.

basis: thanks and calling on the name
note: The people give thanks, call on YHWH's name, and proclaim that his name is exalted; the verse binds invocation, praise, and public announcement in one liturgical act.
The community says its desire is for God's name and memorial while waiting for him; this makes remembrance of the name an inward devotion as well as speech.

basis: lips honoring while the heart is distant
note: Isaiah condemns people whose lips honor God while their hearts are far away; this sharpens the distinction between spoken devotion and inward reality that the commentary develops through loud and hidden.

basis: lips honoring God; heart far away
note: Isaiah distinguishes lip-honor from a distant heart; it illuminates the commentary's insistence that tesbih involves word, action, and intention, and its warning about heedless prayer.

God's house is called a house of prayer for all peoples, where offerings are accepted. This directly pairs prayer with formal communal worship, an important aspect of the commentary's unified tesbih, dhikr, and salat.

basis: the high and lifted One; holy Name; reviving the lowly
note: Isaiah calls God high and lifted up, whose name is Holy, and says that he revives the contrite. This joins the Most High epithet to a divine restoring action relevant to the commentary's praise and purification pairing.

basis: threefold holy acclamation; glory filling earth
note: The seraphim's antiphonal holy acclamation is a heavenly praise formula for YHWH. It offers a liturgical setting for the commentary's tesbih of the transcendent Lord, though it does not reproduce its prayer sequence.

basis: voice of thanksgiving; sacrifice; vowed act
note: Jonah promises sacrifice with a voice of thanksgiving and the fulfilment of vows. This compactly combines vocal praise, gratitude, ritual action, and obedience, all senses the commentary assigns to dhikr and tesbih.

basis: book in the mouth; meditation; doing
note: Joshua is to keep the Torah-book in his mouth, meditate on it day and night, and do it; this closely parallels the commentary's inclusion of recitation, tongue, intention, and obedient action within remembrance.

basis: lifting heart with hands to God
note: Lamentations calls for lifting both heart and hands to God. The explicit union of inward disposition and visible bodily action sharpens the commentary's word-action-intention account of prayer.
The verse forbids profaning the holy Name and calls God the one who sanctifies Israel, sharpening the commentary's 14–15 linkage between a worshipper's prayer and God's purifying action.

basis: Name, sunrise and sunset, pure offering
note: Malachi makes YHWH's name great from sunrise to sunset and connects it with incense and a pure offering; it gathers the commentary's daily praise, Name, ritual action, and 14–15 purification link.
Those who fear YHWH speak with one another, and a memorial book is written for those who esteem his name; this combines spoken remembrance and honoring the name.
Ezra blesses YHWH, the people answer Amen with raised hands, then bow; this makes praise of God a bodily and communal act.

basis: blessing the great God; bowing and face-to-ground worship
note: Ezra blesses YHWH the great God, and the assembly answers, raises hands, bows, and worships with faces to the ground; it is a compact public analogue to praise, utterance, and bodily prayer together.
The Levites read the Torah and explain its sense so hearers understand; this concretely joins recitation and admonition, which the commentary places between the opening command and final prayer.

basis: reading followed by confession and worship
note: The community spends one part of the day reading the Torah and another confessing and worshiping YHWH; this concretely joins recitation and prayer in one service.
The people stand to read Torah and then confess and worship; this concretely parallels the commentary's claim that recitation, admonitory remembrance, and prayer belong to the same devotional work.
The Levites tell the assembly to stand and bless YHWH forever, then bless his glorious name; this joins bodily worship and praise of the name as in the commentary's opening and closing act.

Entering God's courts entails thanksgiving and praise, then giving thanks to him and blessing his name. The verse closely joins the commentary's dhikr as praise and thanks with public worship of the Name.
The speaker blesses YHWH and tells his own soul not to forget God's benefits; this links praise with deliberate remembrance, including the commentary's concern with forgetting.
The verse tells the soul to bless YHWH and not forget his benefits; this is a distinct remembrance claim supporting the commentary's link between worship and avoiding forgetfulness.
The name of YHWH is blessed “from now and forever”; this gives the same enduring verbal praise of the name urged by the commentary.
The psalm calls for the name to be praised from sunrise to sunset; this makes name-praise a repeated daily practice.

basis: Name praised from sunrise to sunset
note: The commentary invokes praise before sunrise and before sunset; this verse explicitly makes the praise of YHWH's name extend from the sun's rising to its setting.

basis: Arabic س ب ح (B001); Hebrew שׁבח
note: The commentary labels Arabic س ب ح as B001. Psalm 117 uses the Hebrew Piel imperative שַׁבְּחוּהוּ, “praise him,” a likely Semitic cognate in a summons for all peoples to praise YHWH.
The psalmist vows not to forget God's word; this is a direct, text-specific counterpart to the commentary's recitation, non-forgetting, and later reminder within the surah's devotional sequence.

basis: lips pouring out praise after instruction
note: The psalmist's lips pour out praise because God teaches statutes. It specifically joins a tongue-level act of praise to received teaching, as the commentary joins Qur'an recitation and dhikr.
The psalmist's tongue sings God's word; this is a precise oral-scriptural parallel to the commentary's statement that reading the Qur'an belongs to remembrance.
The night worshipers lift their hands in the sanctuary and bless YHWH; this is a bodily form of the praise the commentary gathers under prayer.

basis: Hebrew זכר and the enduring name
note: The verse says YHWH's name and memorial endure through generations; זכר is cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label, and directly couples name with remembrance.
The psalm places YHWH's enduring name beside his memorial through all generations; this gives a scriptural counterpart to remembering the Lord's name.
The psalm says YHWH knows a word before it is on the speaker's tongue; this closely matches the claim that God knows what is voiced and concealed.

basis: prayer as incense; lifted hands as evening offering
note: Prayer is likened to incense and raised hands to the evening offering. It supplies a concrete bodily and time-marked analogue to the commentary's prayer as supplication and enacted worship.

basis: prayer as incense and lifted hands
note: The speaker asks that his prayer rise like incense and his lifted hands like an evening offering; this brings spoken supplication and bodily worship into one ritual image.
The psalm ends with the speaker's mouth praising YHWH and all flesh blessing his holy name forever; this joins tongue and name-praise.
The speaker blesses God every day and praises his name forever; this links remembrance and prayer to ongoing praise rather than a single utterance.
One generation is to praise God's works to the next and declare his mighty acts; this is a specific form of recitation and reminder.
The psalm says to praise YHWH's name because it alone is exalted; this directly meets the commentary's command to glorify the Lord's name, “the Most High.”
The psalm closes by calling everything that has breath to praise YHWH; this makes praise an embodied act, fitting the commentary's broad account of tasbih as word and deed.
The prayer asks that both spoken words and inward meditation be acceptable to YHWH; it joins the audible and hidden dimensions of devotion.
The Hebrew verb נַזְכִּיר derives from זכר, cognate with the commentary's Arabic ذ ك ر label; here it means invoking the name of YHWH, not merely recalling information.
The worshiper says “we invoke the name of YHWH our God”; this is a close verbal counterpart to remembering the Lord's name before prayer in 87:15.
The Hebrew calls for thanks to God's holy memorial, using זכר, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label; remembrance here is voiced praise.
The Hebrew זכר (“remember”) is cognate with the commentary's Arabic ذ ك ر label; the psalm uses it for remembering God in bed.
The speaker remembers God on his bed and meditates during the night watches; this develops remembrance as sustained inner devotion, alongside the commentary's spoken remembrance.
The speaker thanks God with the whole heart and glorifies his name forever; this joins inward intention and praise of the name.
The worshipers bow and kneel before YHWH, their maker; this supplies the bodily prostration the commentary includes in prayer, in a creation-focused setting.

basis: bowing and kneeling before the Maker
note: The psalm's invitation to worship, bow down, and kneel gives named bodily acts corresponding to the commentary's standing, bowing, prostration, and supplication as prayer.
The worshiper is told to bless YHWH's name and announce his salvation day after day; this joins repeated remembrance with public praise.

basis: singing to YHWH; blessing the Name day by day
note: The psalm commands singing to YHWH, blessing his name, and proclaiming salvation from day to day; it supplies a distinct psalmic formulation of the commentary's vocal praise, Name, recitation, and recurring practice.

basis: glory due the name and an offering
note: Worshipers ascribe YHWH glory due his name and bring an offering into his courts; this places name-praise and ritual action together.

basis: Hebrew זכר, praise at God's memorial
note: The verse joins singing to YHWH with giving thanks at the memorial of his holiness; its זכר noun is cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label.
The congregation praises YHWH's great and awesome name and calls him holy; the name itself is the object of worship as in 87:1.
The verse commands exalting YHWH and bowing at his footstool; it places praise and bodily prostration together, as the commentary does for tasbih and prayer.

basis: purified speech; calling on the Name; united service
note: God gives peoples a purified lip so that they may call on YHWH's name and serve together; it links the commentary's tongue-bound dhikr, purification, and obedient worship without reducing them to mere speech.
